stem: A company incorporated and hosted entirely in one country sells online to consumers in another, collecting their names and addresses. It has no office, staff or servers in the second country. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The second country's privacy law may still bind it, because modern regimes commonly reach organisations processing residents' data regardless of physical presence
options.why: Extraterritorial reach is the norm in current privacy law. Obligation follows the data subject, not the company's registration.

options.text: Only the law of the country of incorporation applies
options.why: This is the assumption modern privacy law exists to correct. Where you are registered is rarely the test.

options.text: No privacy law applies, since no processing occurs in the second country
options.why: Processing residents' data triggers obligations in many regimes irrespective of where the servers sit.

options.text: Both apply, so the company may choose whichever is less onerous
options.why: Where several apply you meet the strictest obligation. Choosing the weakest is not available.

stem: An organisation operates in a country with a national privacy law, in a state that has passed its own stricter privacy statute. Which applies?

options.text: Both, and the organisation must meet the stricter requirement where they differ
options.why: Regimes stack rather than replace one another. The practical compliance position is the union of obligations, set by whichever is tighter on each point.

options.text: Only the national law, since it has wider jurisdiction
options.why: Wider scope does not mean it overrides. A state or regional law can impose additional duties.

options.text: Only the state law, since it is more specific
options.why: Specificity does not displace the national regime either. Both bind.

options.text: Whichever the organisation names in its privacy policy
options.why: A policy describes your practice. It does not select which laws apply to you.

stem: A compliance team continuously checks control state against its framework and corrects drift before any assessor sees it. A regulator separately requires quarterly figures. Which activities are these?

options.text: Internal monitoring, and external compliance reporting
options.why: Monitoring is your own continuous observation to catch drift. The quarterly submission is reporting, and it is external because the recipient is the regulator.

options.text: External monitoring, and internal compliance reporting
options.why: Reversed. External monitoring is performed by someone outside; the regulator receiving figures is reporting, not monitoring.

options.text: Both are internal monitoring at different intervals
options.why: Sending figures to a regulator is a reporting obligation, not an observation activity.

options.text: Both are attestation
options.why: Attestation is a named individual signing to confirm a state of affairs.

stem: An officer of the company signs a statement confirming that stated controls were in place and operating throughout the period. What does the signature add beyond the report itself?

options.text: Personal accountability: a named individual is now answerable for the accuracy of the claim
options.why: That is why attestation is named separately. A report states a position; an attestation attaches a person to it, with consequences if it is wrong.

options.text: It converts the report into an independent assessment
options.why: Independence comes from who performed the work. An internal officer signing does not supply it.

options.text: It satisfies the requirement for external monitoring
options.why: External monitoring is performed by a party outside the organisation.

options.text: It removes the need for evidence
options.why: The opposite: signing without evidence is how people end up personally exposed.

stem: Why is automation considered an element of effective compliance?

options.text: Continuous automated evidence collection makes compliance a steady state rather than a scramble in the weeks before each assessment
options.why: Manual evidence gathering means you only know your position at audit time. Automation turns that into a current position you can act on.

options.text: Automation removes the need for internal monitoring
options.why: It is how internal monitoring is performed at scale, not a replacement for it.

options.text: Automated systems are exempt from external reporting requirements
options.why: Obligations attach to the organisation regardless of how it gathers its evidence.

options.text: Automation transfers compliance accountability to the tooling vendor
options.why: Accountability cannot be transferred by procuring a tool.

stem: In a compliance programme, what does assigning ownership of a data set achieve that the controller and processor roles do not?

options.text: It names an accountable individual inside the organisation; controller and processor describe the legal relationship between organisations
options.why: Two different axes. The organisation may be the controller, and inside it a named owner is answerable for classification, access decisions and retention.

options.text: It transfers legal accountability to that individual
options.why: The organisation remains accountable in law. Ownership assigns internal responsibility, not statutory liability.

options.text: It determines whether the organisation is a controller or a processor
options.why: That is determined by who decides the purposes and means of processing.

options.text: It satisfies the data subject's right to be forgotten
options.why: That right is satisfied by acting on a request, though having an owner is what makes acting on it possible.

stem: A payment processor suffers a serious compliance failure. Which consequence is imposed by its commercial counterparties rather than by a regulator?

options.text: Contractual impacts, such as penalty clauses or termination by customers
options.why: Contractual consequences flow from agreements with counterparties. Fines, sanctions and loss of licence come from regulators and authorities.

options.text: Fines
options.why: Imposed by a regulator or court under statutory power.

options.text: Loss of licence
options.why: Only an authority that granted the licence can withdraw it.

options.text: Sanctions
options.why: Imposed by government or regulatory bodies.

stem: Which TWO statements about compliance are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: More than one privacy regime can apply to the same record, and the stricter obligation governs
options.why: Regimes stack. Meeting the weakest of several applicable laws is not compliance with any of them.

options.text: Attestation attaches personal accountability to a claim about controls
options.why: A named signature is what separates attestation from a report.

options.text: An organisation with no presence in a territory is outside its privacy law
options.why: Extraterritorial reach is standard in modern privacy regimes.

options.text: Internal monitoring is performed by the regulator
options.why: Internal means your own function. The regulator performs external monitoring.

options.text: Using a compliance automation platform transfers accountability to its vendor
options.why: Responsibility for a task can be delegated; accountability cannot be bought.

stem: A payroll bureau processes a client's staff data as instructed. The bureau then starts using that same data, without the client's agreement, to build and sell salary benchmarking products. What is the bureau's role for that new use?

options.text: The data controller, because it has decided the purpose and means itself
options.why: Role follows who decides why and how data is processed. A processor that sets its own purpose becomes a controller for that use.

options.text: Still the data processor, since the data came from the client
options.why: Where the data came from does not fix the role. The bureau has stepped outside the client's instructions.

options.text: The data owner, because it now holds the dataset
options.why: Data owner is an internal accountability role, not the privacy law term the question is asking for.

options.text: The data custodian, because it stores the data
options.why: Custodian is the internal operational role. The question is about the legal relationship with another organisation.

stem: Before signing with a cloud provider, a company reviews the provider's independent audit reports, financial stability and subcontractor list. What is this activity?

options.text: Due diligence
options.why: Investigation carried out before committing to the relationship is due diligence.

options.text: Due care
options.why: Due care is acting responsibly on an ongoing basis after the commitment, such as monitoring the vendor through the contract.

options.text: An attestation
options.why: An attestation is a formal signed statement that something is true. Reviewing evidence is not the same as signing a statement.

options.text: A right-to-audit clause
options.why: That is a contractual right to inspect later. This is the review performed before signing.

stem: A company reviews its vendor's SOC 2 report annually, checks quarterly that access is still appropriate, and tracks the vendor's security incidents throughout the contract. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: Due care
options.why: Ongoing, reasonable action to maintain the security of the relationship after it has begun is due care.

options.text: Due diligence
options.why: Due diligence was the investigation performed before signing. This is what happens afterwards, continuously.

options.text: A conflict of interest review
options.why: That checks whether the vendor has competing loyalties, which is one narrow part of selection.

options.text: A business impact analysis
options.why: A BIA measures what happens if a process stops. This is vendor oversight.

stem: A regulator can respond to serious or repeated non-compliance with more than a fine. Which of these is a further consequence the regulator itself can impose?

options.text: Loss of the licence to operate in the regulated activity
options.why: Sanctions up to and including withdrawal of a licence are imposed directly by the regulator under its statutory powers.

options.text: A customer ending its contract under a penalty clause
options.why: That is a contractual consequence imposed by a counterparty, not by the regulator.

options.text: Negative press coverage
options.why: Reputational damage arrives through the market. The regulator does not impose it.

options.text: A higher cyber insurance premium at renewal
options.why: A commercial consequence imposed by the insurer, not a regulatory one.

stem: A customer asks a company to erase all personal data it holds about them. Responding accurately requires which capability above all?

options.text: A current data inventory showing where personal data is held
options.why: You cannot erase what you cannot locate. The inventory is what makes a right to be forgotten request answerable at all.

options.text: Full disk encryption on all storage
options.why: Encryption protects data from unauthorised access. It neither locates nor removes it.

options.text: A signed NDA with every processor
options.why: An NDA governs confidentiality. It does not tell you where the data is.

options.text: An annual independent audit
options.why: An audit provides assurance that controls operate. It is not an operational lookup capability.

stem: After a compliance failure the company is fined by the regulator, loses two enterprise renewals, and is criticised in the trade press. Which of these is the direct regulatory consequence?

options.text: The fine
options.why: Only the regulator imposes a fine, under its statutory powers.

options.text: The lost renewals
options.why: A contractual consequence imposed by customers, not the regulator.

options.text: The press criticism
options.why: Reputational damage. Real and often the largest cost, and nobody imposes it.

options.text: All three equally
options.why: They are separated by who imposes the penalty, because that decides who you must satisfy to resolve it.

stem: Staff must confirm each year that they have read and understood the acceptable use policy, and the confirmations must be evidenced to an auditor. What is this?

options.text: Attestation and acknowledgement
options.why: A recorded, signed statement that something is true. It is the evidence an auditor asks for when a control depends on people having been told.

options.text: An internal audit
options.why: An audit tests whether controls operate. Collecting signatures is the control, not the test of it.

options.text: Due diligence
options.why: Due diligence is investigation before committing to a relationship, normally with a third party.

options.text: A right-to-audit clause
options.why: A contractual term letting you inspect a vendor. Unrelated to your own staff.

stem: A customer invokes their right to be forgotten. The company holds their data in a CRM, three backup generations, a data warehouse and a vendor's mailing platform. What determines whether the company can actually comply?

options.text: Whether a current data inventory maps every location the data is held
options.why: You cannot delete what you cannot find. The inventory is what turns the right into something answerable, including the copies at processors.

options.text: Whether the data is encrypted at rest everywhere
options.why: Encryption protects confidentiality and makes locating and deleting the data no easier.

options.text: Whether the customer can prove their identity to the help desk
options.why: Identity verification is a necessary step and is not what determines whether compliance is possible.

options.text: Whether the vendor signed a non-disclosure agreement
options.why: An NDA governs confidentiality of what was shared. It creates no deletion capability.

stem: A company uses a cloud email provider. A subject access request arrives. Who is accountable for answering it?

options.text: The company, as controller
options.why: The controller determines purpose and means and carries the obligation. The provider assists as processor but the duty does not transfer.

options.text: The cloud provider, as processor
options.why: A processor acts on instruction. Outsourcing the processing does not outsource the accountability.

options.text: Whichever party the contract names, with no default
options.why: Privacy law assigns the duty to the controller by default. A contract allocates work, not accountability.

options.text: The data subject's own employer
options.why: Irrelevant to who holds the data and decided why it is held.

stem: A compliance team produces a quarterly pack for the board and a separate annual submission to the regulator. How do these differ?

options.text: The board pack is internal reporting for oversight; the regulator submission is external reporting against a legal obligation
options.why: Internal reporting informs the organisation's own governance. External reporting discharges a duty to someone outside it, and missing it carries regulatory consequences the board pack does not.

options.text: They are the same report with different formatting
options.why: They answer to different audiences with different consequences for being wrong. The regulator can fine you; the board cannot.

options.text: Only the board pack matters, since the regulator relies on the external audit
options.why: An audit is independent assurance. It does not replace a reporting obligation you hold directly.

options.text: The regulator submission is reputational and the board pack is contractual
options.why: Neither. Reputational damage arrives through the market and contractual impacts come from counterparties; a regulatory filing is neither of those.

stem: A former customer asks the company to erase everything it holds about them. Tax law obliges the company to keep invoices for seven years. The account profile, marketing preferences and support chats have no legal retention requirement. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Erase everything at once, including the invoices, because an erasure request overrides every retention rule
options.why: The right to be forgotten is not absolute. A legal duty to keep records outlasts the request, and deleting the invoices would breach the tax requirement.

options.text: Refuse the whole request, because some of the data must be kept
options.why: A partial legal duty does not cover everything. The data with no retention requirement should still be erased.

options.text: Erase the profile, preferences and chats, keep the invoices for the required period, and tell the customer what was kept and why
options.why: Erasure applies to what the company has no lawful reason to keep. Keeping only the legally required records, and saying so, honors both obligations.

options.text: Keep all of it but stop using it for marketing, because the customer only asked for the data to be forgotten in practice
options.why: Stopping one use is not erasure. Data with no retention requirement has to be deleted when the data subject validly asks.

stem: A regulator gives a company 30 days to show that a data subject's records have been erased. The privacy team finds personal data in the CRM, but cannot say whether marketing exports, a retired survey tool or developer test databases also hold copies. Which missing control is the root cause?

options.text: A maintained data inventory of what personal data is held, where, and for how long
options.why: An organization cannot erase, or even report on, data it does not know it holds. The inventory is the prerequisite for answering any data subject request.

options.text: A stronger encryption standard applied to all personal data at rest in every system
options.why: Encryption protects the copies that exist. It does nothing to reveal which copies there are.

options.text: An annual attestation from the CRM owner confirming that the CRM is compliant
options.why: An attestation confirms the state of one system as its owner sees it. It cannot discover systems nobody has listed.

options.text: A self-service data subject portal where people can submit their requests
options.why: Receiving requests more easily does not help find the data. The team could not locate copies even with a perfect request.

stem: A retailer checked a payment vendor's audit reports, finances and references thoroughly before signing in 2021. Since then nobody has reviewed the vendor's access, reports or incidents, and a breach at the vendor exposes card data. A regulator says the retailer failed to exercise due care. Which statement best explains the finding?

options.text: The pre-contract review was incomplete, because due diligence continues for the whole life of the contract
options.why: That is due care. Due diligence is the investigation before commitment, and this one was thorough. What is missing is the ongoing part.

options.text: Due care is a duty on the vendor alone, so the retailer owed nothing after signing
options.why: A customer that hands over card data keeps a duty to act reasonably to protect it, including watching how the vendor behaves.

options.text: The finding is really about attestation, because the vendor should have signed a statement that its controls were in place
options.why: A signed statement is one input to monitoring. The regulator's point is that no one was acting on the vendor relationship after signing.

options.text: Due diligence was done before the contract, but due care is the continuing duty to act reasonably, and nothing was done after signing
options.why: Diligence is the research before commitment. Care is the ongoing reasonable action that follows: reviewing reports, checking access and responding to incidents.

stem: Enterprise customers will not buy a company's service without independent confirmation that its controls meet a recognized framework. The company already runs thorough quarterly self-assessments and reports the results to its own board. What additional activity satisfies the customers?

options.text: More frequent internal monitoring, with the results published on the company website for customers to read
options.why: Self-assessment, however frequent, is the company assessing itself. Customers asked for independence.

options.text: External monitoring: an independent assessor tests the controls and issues a report customers can rely on
options.why: Independence is what the customers are asking for. A third party's findings carry weight that internal reporting cannot.

options.text: An internal attestation signed by the CISO each quarter confirming that the controls operate as stated
options.why: An officer's statement is still the company speaking about itself. It is internal assurance, not independent confirmation.

options.text: Automating the self-assessments so that their results are collected continuously and reported to the board
options.why: Automation makes internal monitoring faster and more consistent. It does not make it independent.

stem: Which TWO of these correctly classify a consequence of non-compliance? (Choose two.)

options.text: A regulator imposes a monetary penalty: a contractual impact
options.why: A penalty imposed by a regulator is a fine. Contractual impacts come from commercial counterparties under an agreement.

options.text: Customers leave after press coverage of a compliance failure: reputational damage
options.why: Loss of trust and custom after public exposure is reputational damage, and it needs no regulator.

options.text: Withdrawal of the right to operate in a regulated market: reputational damage
options.why: Withdrawing the authorization to operate is loss of license. Reputational damage concerns how others view the company.

options.text: A card brand terminates a merchant's agreement after a failed assessment: a contractual impact
options.why: The consequence comes from a commercial agreement and its terms, not from a regulator.

options.text: A contract clause charging for missed security commitments: a regulatory fine
options.why: A charge written into an agreement is a contractual impact. A regulatory fine is imposed by an authority under law.

stem: A compliance team wants to use automation to make its monitoring more effective. Which THREE uses are sound? (Choose three.)

options.text: Scripts that collect control evidence from the systems of record on a schedule
options.why: Evidence pulled from the source on a schedule is more complete and less open to dispute than screenshots gathered before an audit.

options.text: Marking every control compliant for a year once its latest assessment has passed
options.why: Control state changes. A pass last quarter says nothing about this week, which is why monitoring has to be continuous.

options.text: Continuous configuration checks against the baseline that raise a ticket when a system drifts
options.why: Drift is found when it happens, not at the next audit, and the ticket makes sure someone owns the correction.

options.text: Reminders and tracking of staff policy acknowledgements, with overdue reports to managers
options.why: Chasing and recording acknowledgements is repetitive work that automation does well, and it leaves a record for reporting.

options.text: Letting a script decide, without review, whether a policy exception is acceptable
options.why: Judging whether to accept a risk or an exception is a decision for a named person. Automation can supply the evidence, not take the accountability.

stem: A retention schedule deletes email after three years. The company learns that a former employee is likely to sue, and some relevant mailboxes hold messages from two years ago. What should compliance do?

options.text: Let the schedule run as normal, because deleting on schedule is lawful and already documented in the policy
options.why: Routine deletion is lawful until litigation is anticipated. After that, deleting relevant material can be treated as destroying evidence.

options.text: Suspend deletion for every mailbox in the company, to be safe, until the dispute is over
options.why: A hold should reach the relevant data. Suspending the whole schedule keeps personal data far longer than the retention rules allow.

options.text: Suspend deletion for the relevant mailboxes under a hold until counsel releases it, and keep the schedule for everything else
options.why: A legal hold overrides the schedule for the data that matters to the dispute, and the inventory shows where that data is. Everything else keeps its normal retention.

options.text: Copy the relevant messages to a manager's laptop for safekeeping and let the mailboxes be deleted on schedule
options.why: Moving evidence out of the controlled system breaks its integrity and leaves personal data on an unmanaged device.

stem: A regulator orders a firm to stop taking on new customers until it has fixed its controls. There is no monetary penalty and the firm keeps its license. Which consequence is this?

options.text: A fine
options.why: A fine is a payment. Nothing in the stem requires the firm to pay anything.

options.text: Loss of license
options.why: The firm keeps its authorization. Loss of license ends the right to operate that business altogether.

options.text: A sanction
options.why: A restriction on what the firm may do, short of revoking its license, is a sanction.

options.text: A contractual impact
options.why: The order comes from a regulator under law, not from a commercial counterparty under an agreement.

stem: A company outsources payroll to a provider that processes staff data only on the company's instructions. The provider suffers a breach. The company says the provider is at fault and that it owes staff and the regulator nothing. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Accountability passed to the provider when the processing was outsourced, because the provider now holds the data
options.why: Outsourcing moves the work. The company decided why and how the data is used, so it remains accountable.

options.text: The company is the controller and stays accountable to staff and the regulator, though its contract may let it recover costs
options.why: A contract can allocate cost and duties between the parties. It cannot remove the controller's accountability to data subjects and regulators.

options.text: Responsibility is shared equally by default between the two parties, whoever decides the purposes of the processing
options.why: Responsibility follows the role. The party deciding purposes and means is the controller, and it carries the main accountability.

options.text: The staff are the data owners, so they must pursue the provider directly and the company has no role
options.why: Staff are the data subjects. They hold rights over their data, and the controller is the party answerable for it.

stem: A company reviews its controls only in the month before each annual audit, and keeps finding firewall rules and access reviews that lapsed months earlier. Which change addresses the cause?

options.text: Continuous internal monitoring with automated checks and regular reports to management
options.why: The cause is a gap of months between checks. Continuous monitoring shortens it to days, and regular reports keep owners accountable.

options.text: Ask the external auditor to visit twice a year instead of once, so that more of the year is covered
options.why: A second audit adds independence but is still periodic, so drift would still go unseen for months between visits.

options.text: Have control owners sign a stronger attestation before each audit confirming that every control is in place
options.why: An attestation states what the owner believes at one moment. It does not find a rule that lapsed in March.

options.text: Extend the preparation period before each audit from one month to two so that more can be corrected
options.why: More preparation time before the audit tidies the evidence. It does not stop the controls from lapsing in between.

stem: Which TWO are examples of external compliance reporting? (Choose two.)

options.text: A monthly dashboard of open control gaps sent to the CISO
options.why: The audience is inside the organization, so this is internal reporting.

options.text: A breach notification filed with a regulator
options.why: Reporting a required event to an authority outside the organization is external reporting.

options.text: A weekly summary of overdue tickets sent to operations managers
options.why: Internal operational reporting. Nothing leaves the organization.

options.text: An annual compliance certificate filed with an industry regulator
options.why: A formal submission to an outside body, as a regulation requires, is external reporting.

options.text: A quarterly update on policy exceptions presented to the audit committee
options.why: The audit committee is part of the organization's own governance, so this is internal reporting.

stem: Which TWO activities are examples of due care rather than due diligence? (Choose two.)

options.text: Reviewing a prospective supplier's financial statements before signing
options.why: Researching a supplier before commitment is due diligence.

options.text: Applying security patches on the schedule the company's own policy sets
options.why: Due care is acting on a continuing basis the way a reasonable organization would. Keeping to its own patching policy is a clear example.

options.text: Assessing the security of a company before acquiring it
options.why: Investigating a target before committing is due diligence.

options.text: Reviewing a vendor's access rights every quarter after the contract is signed
options.why: Checking, after signing, that the arrangement is still appropriate is continuing, reasonable action, which is due care.

options.text: Requesting references from three of a supplier's customers during selection
options.why: A selection-stage investigation is due diligence.

stem: A customer asks a company to delete the personal data it holds about them. In privacy law terms, who is the customer?

options.text: The data controller
options.why: The controller decides why and how the data is processed. That is the company here.

options.text: The data processor
options.why: A processor handles data on behalf of the controller. The customer does neither.

options.text: The data custodian
options.why: A custodian looks after data on the owner's behalf. The customer is the person the data is about.

options.text: The data subject
options.why: The person the personal data identifies is the data subject, and this is the person who holds the deletion right.
